virals.hook:
Why More Strikes Against the Basij Would Not Have Brought Down Iran’s Regime

I think this study misses a crucial point about the war against Iran and, more importantly, about the fundamental limitations of attempting regime change through airpower.

First, every military operation against Iran is extremely complex. The number of targets that can be attacked is not unlimited, and target selection must reflect clear operational priorities and realistic strategic objectives. Striking one category of targets inevitably comes at the expense of another.

Second, once it became clear that the Kurdish option was collapsing, the possibility of bringing down the Iranian regime became even more remote(Not that it was realistic from the beginning).

More importantly, this decision had clarified the fundamental nature of the campaign: it was a war aimed at weakening the regime, not overthrowing it. That distinction matters enormously.

Once regime change was no longer a realistic objective, the operational emphasis naturally shifted toward severely degrading the regime's military production infrastructure, eliminating senior commanders, and weakening its broader military capabilities, rather than prioritizing attacks on Basij facilities and other instruments of domestic control.

But it would also be wrong to suggest that Israel / US completely ignored the regime's internal security apparatus.

Israeli strikes did target Basij headquarters and facilities, and senior figures within the organization were reportedly eliminated, including its commander, Soleimani, his deputy and senior intelligence officials.

The problem was that the Iranian regime had anticipated precisely this scenario. It had prepared to evacuate facilities, disperse personnel, and continue operating from alternative locations, including schools and other civilian buildings.

The fundamental problem was not the selection of targets. It was the assumption that airstrikes could somehow persuade or enable the Iranian population to rise up and overthrow the regime.

That assumption was deeply flawed. Iran has no sufficiently organized opposition capable of translating military pressure into a coordinated political uprising. There was no credible mechanism for turning the destruction of security facilities into the collapse of the regime's control over the country.

Even if Israel and the United States had devoted significantly more resources to attacking Basij headquarters, command centers, and other institutions of domestic repression, the fundamental political reality would not have changed.

The regime retained its coercive capabilities, its organizational structure, and its determination to survive. Meanwhile, ordinary Iranians were living through a war, facing uncertainty, destruction, and the dangers of continued bombardment.

Under those circumstances, expecting civilians to take to the streets and confront an entrenched security apparatus, without an organized opposition or a credible alternative leadership, was never a realistic strategy.

Airpower can destroy buildings, eliminate commanders, and weaken military capabilities. But it cannot create an organized opposition, establish alternative political leadership, or manufacture the conditions for a successful popular revolution.

That is why I disagree with the suggestion that a different target list, focused more heavily on the Basij, could have produced regime change.

The issue was never simply whether enough Basij facilities had been destroyed. It was whether there was any realistic political mechanism through which those attacks could bring down the Islamic Republic. There was not.

And that is the central lesson: the failure to overthrow the Iranian regime was not primarily a failure of targeting. It reflected the absence of the political and organizational conditions necessary for regime change.

More bombs against the Basij would not have solved that problem.

#IranWar‌ 
#iran

outsiders.hook:
The next 15 days. A simple day-by-day prediction. Bookmark this.
Trump just lost the House and the Senate. His own vice president said it plainly: “We lost because of this war.”
Netanyahu also lost his majority in Israel. His side still doesn’t have enough seats to control the government.
Both leaders have been weakened by this war. They have less to lose now and fewer reasons to hold back.

Next 48 hours:

The U.S. military already has a 3-day strike plan ready. Three aircraft carriers are in the area.
Trump said, “We are ready to go.” I don’t believe the claim that there are “no plans for immediate action.”

Days 3–4
First strikes hit Iran’s missile bases, drone factories, IRGC command centers, and energy sites.
Iran hits back at U.S. bases, Saudi oil facilities, and UAE refineries.
Oil jumps overnight from about $102 to $150 a barrel.

Days 5–7

They go after “Pickaxe Mountain,” the deep underground site near Natanz. Trump has already named this place.
Regular bombs probably can’t destroy it, which is why people are talking about using a nuclear weapon.
Iranian TV has started telling its 90 million people what to do if they see a bright flash.

Days 8–10

Iran still has 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%. That’s enough material for roughly 10 nuclear bombs.
Some Iranian lawmakers want to push enrichment up to 90%.
Iran shuts down the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis block the Red Sea. Two major oil routes are cut off at the same time.
Oil hits $200 a barrel.

Days 11–13

Gas prices in the U.S. go over $8 a gallon. Airlines cut flights. Trucks stop moving.
Japan, South Korea, and India start running out of fuel.
The stock market goes from a correction to a full crash.

Days 14–15

The new Congress tries to cut off war funding (even though they don’t officially take power until January).
Netanyahu stays in office as a “wartime prime minister.” Leaders don’t usually get replaced in the middle of a war.
There are only two outcomes for that uranium: it gets destroyed, or it gets turned into bombs. There is no third option.
They lost the elections. Now they have to win this war before January.
This is my read of the situation. Every step above is based on plans, targets, or statements that have already been made.
Bookmark this and check back around November 25 to see how close it was.
Some sources are calling this week “the calm before negotiations.” I’ll keep posting what I see without spinning it either way. Share this with anyone who thinks the war is about to cool off.

outsiders.name: Danny (Dennis) Citrinowicz ,داني سيترينوفيتش
outsiders.hook:
Why More Strikes Against the Basij Would Not Have Brought Down Iran’s Regime

I think this study misses a crucial point about the war against Iran and, more importantly, about the fundamental limitations of attempting regime change through airpower.

First, every military operation against Iran is extremely complex. The number of targets that can be attacked is not unlimited, and target selection must reflect clear operational priorities and realistic strategic objectives. Striking one category of targets inevitably comes at the expense of another.

Second, once it became clear that the Kurdish option was collapsing, the possibility of bringing down the Iranian regime became even more remote(Not that it was realistic from the beginning).

More importantly, this decision had clarified the fundamental nature of the campaign: it was a war aimed at weakening the regime, not overthrowing it. That distinction matters enormously.

Once regime change was no longer a realistic objective, the operational emphasis naturally shifted toward severely degrading the regime's military production infrastructure, eliminating senior commanders, and weakening its broader military capabilities, rather than prioritizing attacks on Basij facilities and other instruments of domestic control.

But it would also be wrong to suggest that Israel / US completely ignored the regime's internal security apparatus.

Israeli strikes did target Basij headquarters and facilities, and senior figures within the organization were reportedly eliminated, including its commander, Soleimani, his deputy and senior intelligence officials.

The problem was that the Iranian regime had anticipated precisely this scenario. It had prepared to evacuate facilities, disperse personnel, and continue operating from alternative locations, including schools and other civilian buildings.

The fundamental problem was not the selection of targets. It was the assumption that airstrikes could somehow persuade or enable the Iranian population to rise up and overthrow the regime.

That assumption was deeply flawed. Iran has no sufficiently organized opposition capable of translating military pressure into a coordinated political uprising. There was no credible mechanism for turning the destruction of security facilities into the collapse of the regime's control over the country.

Even if Israel and the United States had devoted significantly more resources to attacking Basij headquarters, command centers, and other institutions of domestic repression, the fundamental political reality would not have changed.

The regime retained its coercive capabilities, its organizational structure, and its determination to survive. Meanwhile, ordinary Iranians were living through a war, facing uncertainty, destruction, and the dangers of continued bombardment.

Under those circumstances, expecting civilians to take to the streets and confront an entrenched security apparatus, without an organized opposition or a credible alternative leadership, was never a realistic strategy.

Airpower can destroy buildings, eliminate commanders, and weaken military capabilities. But it cannot create an organized opposition, establish alternative political leadership, or manufacture the conditions for a successful popular revolution.

That is why I disagree with the suggestion that a different target list, focused more heavily on the Basij, could have produced regime change.

The issue was never simply whether enough Basij facilities had been destroyed. It was whether there was any realistic political mechanism through which those attacks could bring down the Islamic Republic. There was not.

And that is the central lesson: the failure to overthrow the Iranian regime was not primarily a failure of targeting. It reflected the absence of the political and organizational conditions necessary for regime change.

More bombs against the Basij would not have solved that problem.

#IranWar‌ 
#iran
